1.title: Data Security: Handling and Encryption
1.text: Welcome to Module thirteen: Data Security: Handling and Encryption. It covers the exam area five. Security Operations and Incident Response. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. five point one Understand data security: Data handling (for example classification, labeling, masking, and sanitization). Encryption (for example symmetric, asymmetric, hashing, quantum resistant cryptography). Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: five. Security Operations and Incident Response (seventeen point three percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: Data classification and labeling
1.text: Data classification and labeling. Classification sorts data by sensitivity, so each level gets matching protection. Labeling marks the data (file, email, document) with its level so people and systems treat it correctly.

1.title: Data classification and labeling, continued
1.text: Data classification and labeling. The figure shows this: Data handling stages and the classification levels.

1.title: Data classification and labeling, continued
1.text: Data classification and labeling. Public. Meaning: No harm if disclosed. Example: Press release. Internal (private). Meaning: For staff only. Example: Internal memo. Confidential (sensitive). Meaning: Serious harm if disclosed. Example: Customer records, contracts. Restricted (secret). Meaning: Severe harm if disclosed. Example: Trade secrets, health data. The data owner decides the classification; the custodian runs the protection. Classification drives access, encryption and retention. Exam tip: The data owner classifies; the custodian protects. Unlabeled data is hard to protect: label it.

1.title: The data life cycle and handling
1.text: The data life cycle and handling. Create or collect. Classify and collect only what is needed (minimization). Store. Encrypt, control access, back up. Use. Least privilege, monitoring. Share. Approved channels only, encryption, data loss prevention. Archive. Retain as law and policy require. Destroy. Sanitize so data cannot be recovered. Data states: at rest (stored), in transit (moving), in use (being processed). Encrypt at rest and in transit. A I workspaces: staff must not paste confidential data into public A I tools because of data leakage; classify and mask data first.

1.title: Masking and sanitization
1.text: Masking and sanitization. Masking. Hides part of a value (a card shown as X X X X one thousand two hundred thirty-four); the original stays in the source. Tokenization. Replaces a value with a random token; the real value is stored elsewhere. Sanitization. Removes data from media so it cannot be recovered. Clear. Overwrite the data; fine for reuse inside the organization. Purge. Stronger methods (degauss, cryptographic erase); media may be reused. Destroy. Physical destruction (shred, incinerate); highest assurance. Exam tip: Deleting a file is not sanitizing. Destroy for the highest assurance. Cryptographic erase means destroying the key.

1.title: Encryption basics
1.text: Encryption basics. Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext with an algorithm and a key. It protects confidentiality. Symmetric (for example A E S). Keys: One shared key. Speed: Fast. Use: Bulk data, disks, V P N (virtual private network) traffic. Asymmetric (for example R S A, E C C). Keys: Key pair: public and private. Speed: Slower. Use: Key exchange, digital signatures. Hashing (for example S H A two hundred fifty-six). Keys: No key; one-way. Speed: Fast. Use: Integrity, password storage (with salt).

1.title: Encryption basics, continued
1.text: Encryption basics. Encrypt with the receiver's public key; only the private key decrypts. Confidentiality with asymmetric keys. Sign with your private key; anyone verifies with your public key. Authenticity and non-repudiation. Hash cannot be reversed; the same input always gives the same hash. Integrity check. Key management. Protect, rotate and back up keys; a lost key means lost data. Public key infrastructure (P K I) uses certificates issued by a certificate authority to bind a public key to an identity. T L S protects data in transit on the web. Quantum-resistant (post-quantum) cryptography means algorithms designed to withstand quantum computers, which could break R S A and E C C. Organizations plan to move to them. Exam tip: Symmetric equals one key, fast. Asymmetric equals key pair, slower. Hash equals no key, one way. Hashing is not encryption.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Who decides the classification level of a set of customer records? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: The data owner, who is accountable for the data. The data owner decides the classification; the custodian applies the protection.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which technology is best for encrypting a large database quickly? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Symmetric encryption such as A E S. Symmetric encryption is fast and suits bulk data.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A user wants to prove that a file was not changed during download. What should be compared? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: The hash value of the file. A hash gives an integrity check: if the hash is the same, the file is unchanged.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A hard disk with sensitive data is retired and the data must be impossible to recover. Which method gives the highest assurance? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Physically destroying the disk. Physical destruction gives the highest assurance of sanitization.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A customer service tool shows only the last four digits of a card number. What technique is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Masking of the sensitive value. Showing only part of a value hides the rest from the viewer, which is masking.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which risk makes organizations plan for quantum-resistant cryptography? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Quantum computers may break R S A and E C C. Quantum computers could break current asymmetric algorithms such as R S A and E C C.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. How many keys does symmetric encryption use? Answer: One shared key. Question two. Which key decrypts a message encrypted with the receiver's public key? Answer: The receiver's private key. Question three. What does a digital signature use to sign? Answer: The sender's private key.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Is hashing reversible? Answer: No, it is one way. Question five. What are the three data states? Answer: At rest, in transit, in use. Question six. What are the three sanitization methods? Answer: Clear, purge, destroy.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Classification: public, internal, confidential, restricted; owner decides, custodian protects. Data states: at rest, in transit, in use; encrypt at rest and in transit. Masking or tokenization: hide part of a value or replace with a token. Sanitization: clear, purge, destroy; deleting is not sanitizing. Encryption: symmetric one key; asymmetric key pair; hash one way. Signatures: sign with private key, verify with public key. Quantum: plan quantum-resistant algorithms.
